Heritage walk in Ahmedabad: pols, mosques and stepwells

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A heritage walk in Ahmedabad goes through the walled old city founded by Sultan Ahmad Shah I in 1411: Bhadra Fort, Teen Darwaza, the Jama Masjid, the pols (gated residential lanes) with their carved wooden houses, Jain and Swaminarayan temples, and Sidi Saiyyed Mosque. The Historic City of Ahmadabad became a UNESCO site in 2017.

We arrange heritage walks in Ahmedabad's old city on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Ahmedabad matters: India's first World Heritage City

In 2017 the walled city of Ahmedabad became the first Indian city to be inscribed as a whole on the UNESCO World Heritage List, as the Historic City of Ahmadabad. What UNESCO recognised was not a single monument but an urban fabric: Sultanate mosques and tombs set inside a dense grid of pols, where Hindu, Jain and Muslim communities have lived, traded and worshipped side by side for six centuries.

That makes Ahmedabad one of the best places in India to teach what a historic city is. A walk here is about house types, water, guilds, street names and festivals as much as about famous buildings. It also raises current questions: how a living old city keeps its timber houses standing, and who pays for their repair. The lecture Who owns the past? takes up exactly this debate.

Layers of history in Ahmedabad

The site on the east bank of the Sabarmati was settled long before the sultans. An earlier town called Ashaval or Karnavati, associated with the Chaulukya (Solanki) rulers of the 11th century, lay nearby, though its exact extent is still discussed by historians.

Sultan Ahmad Shah I of the Gujarat Sultanate founded the new capital in 1411, beginning with the citadel of Bhadra. Over the next century his successors built some of the finest mosques in India, mixing local temple-building traditions (carved pillars, corbelled domes, stone jali) with the plan of a congregational mosque. The Jama Masjid of 1424 and the jali windows of Sidi Saiyyed Mosque (about 1572 to 1573) are the best known results. Our guide to Indo-Islamic architecture places these buildings in a wider Indian story.

The Mughals took Gujarat in 1572 to 1573, and Ahmedabad became a great textile and trading city under them, then under the Marathas from the mid 18th century, and the British from 1817. From the 1860s cotton mills made it the 'Manchester of the East'. In 1915 Gandhi set up his first ashram in the city, moving to the Sabarmati site in 1917. After independence, Le Corbusier, Louis Kahn and Charles Correa added modern buildings that are now heritage too.

Places a heritage walk in Ahmedabad covers

  1. Bhadra Fort 1411

    The first citadel of Ahmad Shah I. Look at the gateway and the Bhadrakali shrine inside.

  2. Teen Darwaza 1415

    Triple gateway that once led from the citadel to the royal square; the market around it is busy all day.

  3. Jama Masjid 1424

    Congregational mosque with 260 pillars and a prayer hall that borrows from local temple design.

  4. Tomb of Ahmad Shah (Badshah no Hajiro) 15th century

    Tomb of the city's founder, just east of the Jama Masjid, with fine stone screens.

  5. Rani no Hajiro 15th century

    Tombs of the royal women, now surrounded by a market lane.

  6. Manek Chowk 15th century onward

    Old market square; a jewellers' market by day and a food market at night.

  7. Sidi Saiyyed Mosque About 1572 to 1573

    Famous for its carved stone jali of an intertwined tree, now an informal symbol of the city.

  8. Doshiwada ni Pol 17th to 19th century houses

    A cluster of pols with carved wooden facades, chabutros and community temples.

  9. Mahurat Pol Traditionally said to be the first pol

    A good place to explain how gates, tanks and shared spaces work.

  10. Kalupur Swaminarayan Temple 1822

    First temple of the Swaminarayan sect, with brightly painted carved wood.

  11. Hutheesing Jain Temple 1848

    White marble temple built by a merchant family, just outside Delhi Darwaza.

  12. Sidi Bashir Mosque (Shaking Minarets) 15th century

    Only the minarets survive, known for transmitting vibration from one to the other.

  13. Dada Harir Stepwell About 1499 to 1500

    Five-level stepwell in Asarwa with Sanskrit and Arabic inscriptions.

  14. Adalaj Stepwell 1499

    Ornate stepwell north of the city; a vehicle is needed.

  15. Sarkhej Roza 15th century

    Tomb, mosque and tank complex south-west of the city; a vehicle is needed.

  16. Sabarmati Ashram 1917

    Gandhi's home from 1917 to 1930 and the starting point of the Dandi March.

Walking routes in Ahmedabad

The Sultanate core on foot

About 2 hours

Bhadra Fort → Teen Darwaza → Jama Masjid → Tomb of Ahmad Shah (Badshah no Hajiro) → Rani no Hajiro → Manek Chowk → Sidi Saiyyed Mosque

Pols and temples morning walk

About 2.5 hours

Kalupur Swaminarayan Temple → Mahurat Pol → Doshiwada ni Pol → Manek Chowk → Jama Masjid

Stepwells, rozas and the ashram (vehicle needed)

Half a day

Hutheesing Jain Temple → Dada Harir Stepwell → Adalaj Stepwell → Sabarmati Ashram → Sarkhej Roza

Museums in Ahmedabad

  • Calico Museum of Textiles. One of the finest textile collections in India, in the Sarabhai family's Shahibaug estate. Visits are by guided tour with limited places, so book well ahead.
  • Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya. The Sabarmati Ashram museum, designed by Charles Correa, on Gandhi's life and the freedom movement.
  • Lalbhai Dalpatbhai Museum. Sculpture, manuscripts, paintings and bronzes, with strong Jain and western Indian holdings.
  • Sanskar Kendra (City Museum). A Le Corbusier building in Paldi that tells the story of Ahmedabad.

Best time for a walk

November to February. Walks in the old city begin around 7.30 to 8 am, before heat and traffic; avoid the hottest months of April to June.

Walking the pols: what to look for

A pol is a gated street or cluster of houses, usually home to people of one caste, occupation or community. Each has a main gate, often a small temple, a well or underground water tank, and a chabutro: a raised, carved bird feeder on a pillar. Houses are built in timber and brick with carved brackets, balconies and painted facades, and many have an internal courtyard and a tank below the floor for rainwater.

On a pol walk you read the details: the iron ring on a gate, a guild inscription, a secret passage between two lanes, the date on a house, or the change in style from Gujarati wood carving to 19th century colonial cast iron and stucco. Doshiwada ni Pol, Mahurat Pol and the lanes around Manek Chowk are common starting points. Walks start early, when the lanes are cool and residents are going about their morning.

Because pol houses are private homes, groups keep to the street, keep voices low and photograph only with permission. Many students find the conversations with residents the best part. An oral history and neighbourhood memory lab can turn this into a structured class project.

Ahmedabad heritage walk for schools and groups

The old city walk is about 2 kilometres and works for classes 5 and above. Younger groups can do a 90 minute version that stays within a few pols and ends at the Jama Masjid. Wear modest clothing and carry scarves; shoes come off at mosques and temples.

Sarkhej Roza, Adalaj stepwell and the Sabarmati Ashram are outside the walled city and need a vehicle. They can be added as a half day. Ahmedabad also makes a good base for a longer study tour of Gujarat: the Harappan Gujarat journey covers Lothal and Dholavira, and a day at Champaner and Pavagadh shows another Sultanate capital, abandoned rather than still lived in.

Talaash Heritage arranges the walk on request with an archaeologist or historian and can begin with a short classroom lecture on how cities grow. For school-level depth on water systems, our guide to stepwells of India is a useful pre-reading.

Beyond the walls: stepwells, rozas and modern heritage

Adalaj stepwell, built in 1499 by Rani Rudabai, wife of a Vaghela chief, is five storeys deep with carved landings and octagonal openings. Dada Harir stepwell inside the city, built around 1499 to 1500, is plainer and less crowded. Both show how Gujarat turned a practical water source into public architecture.

Sarkhej Roza, a complex of tomb, mosque and tank built in the 15th century around the shrine of the Sufi saint Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh, is a calm, open contrast to the old city. Later layers include the Sabarmati Ashram and its museum by Charles Correa, and the Indian Institute of Management campus by Louis Kahn, both worth seeing for older students of architecture.

Questions people ask

What is a pol in Ahmedabad?

A pol is a gated residential street or cluster of houses in the old city, traditionally home to one community or occupation. It usually has a main gate, a temple, a water tank, and a chabutro bird feeder. There are several hundred pols inside the old walls.

Why is Ahmedabad a UNESCO World Heritage City?

UNESCO inscribed the Historic City of Ahmadabad in 2017 for its Sultanate-period mosques and tombs and its pols with timber houses, which together show a city where several communities have lived and built side by side since 1411.

What are the main historical places in Ahmedabad?

Bhadra Fort, Teen Darwaza, the Jama Masjid, Sidi Saiyyed Mosque, the shaking minarets, the pols, the Hutheesing and Swaminarayan temples, Dada Harir and Adalaj stepwells, Sarkhej Roza and the Sabarmati Ashram.

Is the Ahmedabad heritage walk suitable for schools?

Yes. The old city route is about 2 kilometres on level ground. Classes 5 and up manage the full walk; younger children do a shorter loop. Students should dress modestly and be ready to remove shoes at religious buildings.

Do I need a vehicle?

Not for the walled city. You need one for Adalaj, Sarkhej Roza, the Sabarmati Ashram and the Calico Museum, which are spread across the city.
